title: Profiling with DevTools
objectives: Follow the record → read the flame chart → find the culprit workflow
Read a Network waterfall to attribute time to requests
Localize a memory leak with snapshot comparisons
Write performance.now() micro-benchmarks that do not lie to you
body:
Profiling is a workflow, not a panel you glance at: reproduce the problem on a production-like build, record it, read the flame chart top-down for the tasks that own the frame budget, then zoom into the widest stack and read it bottom-up to find the code to blame. Everything else — hunches, console.time sprinkles, micro-benchmarks — only supports that loop.

## The problem
Users report the search page freezing. On your machine it is fine. You need a repeatable way to capture the jank, attribute it to code, and later prove a fix worked — without trusting feelings or one-off timing prints.

## Constraints
- Dev builds run different code than production: minified, tree-shaken, sometimes faster. Profile a production build (or one with the same flags).
- The flame chart: width is time, height is stack depth; the widest bars at the top of a long task are where the time is.
- The Network panel orders by start time — a request that *starts* late is usually blocked by an earlier one, not slow itself.
- Micro-benchmarks lie through JIT warmup, dead-code elimination and noise unless you control for them.

## Options
Three profiling modes for three questions:

```js
// Micro: does function A beat B in isolation? (with traps handled)
function bench(fn, samples = 50) {
  fn(); fn();                       // warmup: let the JIT compile it
  const times = []
  for (let i = 0; i < samples; i++) {
    const t0 = performance.now()
    fn()
    times.push(performance.now() - t0)
  }
  times.sort((a, b) => a - b)
  return times[Math.floor(samples / 2)] // median resists outliers
}
```
Macro: the Performance panel answers *where does the time go in this interaction*. Memory: heap snapshots answer *what accumulates*. Choose the tool after you have phrased the question — micro-benchmarks cannot find a layout thrash, and a flame chart cannot find a leak.

## Tradeoffs
Micro-benchmarks are cheap and precise but measure a synthetic world: inlining and optimization can make A win in isolation while B wins in the app. Full traces are realistic but heavy — profiling itself adds overhead, so keep recordings to a few seconds around the exact interaction. Heap snapshots are exact but large; compare them, do not read them raw.

## Decision
For user-facing jank, start with a Performance recording on a production build; only drop to micro-benchmarks for the specific function the trace blamed. For leaks, go straight to snapshots. Always re-run the same recording after the fix — the after trace is the deliverable.

## Measure it
The discipline: record before (baseline) → change one thing → record after → compare task durations, layout counts, and script time in the same conditions. In micro-benchmarks, report median over many samples with warmup, and distrust any difference under ~10% or under the timer's noise floor.

## Best practices
- Profile production builds; keep one interaction per recording.
- Read the flame chart for the widest stacks first, then expand downward.
- In the waterfall, ask why a request started late before asking why it was slow.
- Use median (not mean) and warmup in micro-benchmarks.
- Save before/after traces with the change that produced them.

## Common mistakes
- Profiling a dev server with source maps and blaming the optimizer's artifacts.
- Trusting a micro-benchmark with three samples and no warmup — that measures noise and JIT cold start.
- Optimizing a function that the flame chart never shows inside a real frame.
- Taking one heap snapshot and reading it like a novel instead of diffing two.
- Declaring victory without an after recording that shows the long task gone.

examples.name: micro-bench.js

exercise.prompt: Build a benchmark-trustworthiness analyzer. Two candidate optimizations report their median ms, p90 ms and sample count. For each, render a verdict: trustworthy-faster only when it has at least 30 samples AND its median is at least 10% lower than the baseline; low-samples when under 30 samples; noise when the median delta is under 10%. Implement the verdict logic.
hints: Check sample count first: under 30 samples cannot be trusted regardless of the median.
Then compare medians: (baseline.median - c.median) / baseline.median must be at least 0.10.
Order matters — a fast result from 8 samples is still low-samples.

questions.prompt: Why should micro-benchmarks run the measured function a few times before timing it?
options: To fill the CPU cache with the benchmark's own code only
To give the JIT time to compile and optimize it, so you measure steady state
To raise the timer resolution of performance.now()
To warm the network connection used by the function
questions.explanation: The first executions include interpretation and JIT compilation; without warmup you mostly measure the optimizer, not the code.

questions.prompt: In the Network waterfall, a request starts 900 ms after navigation. What should you investigate first?
options: The server latency of that request
Which earlier resource or script discovery chain delayed its start
Whether HTTP/3 is enabled on the origin
questions.explanation: A late start is a scheduling/discovery problem — something earlier (a script, a chained import, preload absence) gated it; the request itself may be perfectly fast.
